pedagogy.summary: This topic builds from the triangle angle sum (180°) to the general interior-angle sum of any polygon, (n−2)×180°, DERIVED by splitting the polygon into n−2 triangles, and to the interior/exterior angle relationship (they sum to 180° at each vertex; all exterior angles sum to 360° for any polygon). Best taught by deriving the formulas from structure — partitioning into triangles, walking the perimeter to feel the 360° of turning — rather than memorising them, and by carefully separating the two 'totals' pupils confuse: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex, versus all exterior angles = 360° for the WHOLE polygon. For regular polygons each angle is the sum divided by n, but this division applies ONLY when the polygon is regular.
bestPractices: Derive (n−2)×180° by splitting the polygon into triangles from one vertex (a hexagon → 4 triangles → 720°); don't present the formula as a rule to memorise
Distinguish demonstration from proof: tearing off a triangle's corners to form a straight line DEMONSTRATES 180° but is not a proof — pupils should also meet the deductive argument
Keep the two exterior-angle totals apart: interior + exterior = 180° at a single vertex; the sum of ALL exterior angles is 360° for any polygon, however many sides

Attach the word 'regular' to every ÷n formula: each interior angle = sum ÷ n and each exterior = 360 ÷ n hold ONLY for regular polygons; for an irregular one, find a missing angle by subtracting known angles from the sum
Use the 'walking the perimeter' turning model to make the 360° total of exterior angles concrete
Stress that the angle sum depends on the NUMBER OF SIDES, not on the size of the polygon
keyRepresentations: Polygon partitioned into triangles from one vertex (n sides → n−2 triangles)
Torn-off triangle corners arranged on a straight line (demonstration of 180°)
A marker 'walking the perimeter', turning through 360° in total (exterior angles)
Interior and exterior angle pair at a vertex sitting on a straight line (sum 180°)
A regular polygon with equal angles beside an irregular one with the same sum but unequal angles
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a triangle's angles sum to 360°
Dividing 360° (or the interior sum) by n for an IRREGULAR polygon, or assuming all its angles are equal
Believing a bigger polygon has a bigger angle sum (angle scales with size)
Reporting the interior-angle SUM as though it were one interior angle (forgetting to divide by n)

learn.summary: Pupils (ages 11–14) derive the interior-angle sum of a polygon by splitting it into n−2 triangles from one vertex ((n−2)×180°), feel the exterior-angle total of 360° by walking the perimeter, and carefully separate the two 'totals' they confuse: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex, versus all exterior angles = 360° for the WHOLE polygon. Dividing by n (sum÷n for each interior, 360÷n for each exterior) gives each angle ONLY when all the angles are equal. This is true of every regular polygon (the KS3 focus), and also of equal-angled shapes such as a non-square rectangle. The angle sum depends on the number of sides, not the polygon's size. The strongest route is proposed to be a construction the child performs (triangulate, walk the perimeter, toggle regular/irregular); fixed diagrams and scored questions are useful support with stated limits.

activities.title: Triangulate to build the angle sum
feedback: If a learner says the sum should be bigger for a physically larger polygon, enlarge the same shape with its angles unchanged and ask whether any angle changed — the sum depends only on the number of sides.

If a learner counts n triangles instead of n−2, ask them to look at the two sides meeting at the chosen vertex and check whether every side became the base of its own triangle; the two sides at the chosen vertex do not, which is why the count is n−2.
An optional running tally showing '(n−2)×180' as diagonals are drawn makes the link between triangle count and total concrete; this is a support, not a requirement.
activities.rationale: Deriving the formula from triangulation rather than memorising it targets the topic's core structure and the documented size-independence misconception. Learner-performed partitioning with immediate confirmation is proposed as the strongest route; fixed diagrams can show one split but cannot let the child vary n.
sourceClaims: The interior angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n−2)×180°, derived by splitting the polygon into n−2 triangles each summing to 180° (quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°); an exterior angle is on a straight line with its interior angle so they sum to 180°; the sum of all exterior angles is 360° (from 180n − (n−2)×180 = 360); students often confuse a demonstration for a proof

Children (and educated adults) tend to judge a triangle's missing angle as scaling with the triangle's size, contradicting the size-independent angle sum — they reason by mental simulation rather than by the rule
KS3 pupils should derive and use the sum of interior angles of a polygon and the fact that the exterior angles of a polygon sum to 360°
learnerActions: Start with a polygon whose number of sides you can change. Before calculating, predict: what do all its interior angles add to?
Split the polygon into triangles by drawing diagonals from one corner. Count the triangles: a pentagon gives 3, a hexagon gives 4.
Record the running total as (number of triangles)×180°: pentagon 3×180 = 540°, hexagon 4×180 = 720°.
State the general pattern in your own words: splitting from one corner, a convex n-sided polygon always makes n−2 triangles, so the interior sum is (n−2)×180°.
Add two more sides and confirm the sum GROWS with the number of sides — not with the polygon's size.
activities.intendedInsight: The interior-angle sum (n−2)×180° is a consequence of how many triangles the polygon decomposes into, and it depends on the number of sides, not the size.

activities.title: Walk the perimeter: exterior angles total 360°
feedback: If a learner says more sides should give a bigger exterior total, have them walk two different polygons and compare: both complete exactly one full turn (360°).
If a learner reports 360° at a single vertex, point to the straight line at that corner: the interior and its exterior together make 180° there.
An optional mode that accumulates each turn as the marker strides round makes 'one full turn = 360°' concrete; keep it as an illustration, not the only way to reach the result.
activities.rationale: The perimeter-walk turning model makes the 360° exterior total tangible and directly separates the two totals pupils confuse. The exterior sum of 360° regardless of sides is supported by sources (convex KS3 case); the single-vertex 180° pairing is a distinct relationship.
sourceClaims: The interior angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n−2)×180°, derived by splitting the polygon into n−2 triangles each summing to 180° (quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°); an exterior angle is on a straight line with its interior angle so they sum to 180°; the sum of all exterior angles is 360° (from 180n − (n−2)×180 = 360); students often confuse a demonstration for a proof

Students commonly confuse interior and exterior angles; they wrongly assume all exterior angles are equal or that more sides means a bigger exterior sum (it is always 360° regardless of the number of sides); the formula 360÷n gives each exterior angle ONLY for a regular polygon — irregular polygons still total 360° but each angle must be found individually
KS3 pupils should derive and use the sum of interior angles of a polygon and the fact that the exterior angles of a polygon sum to 360°
learnerActions: Imagine (or move a marker) walking around the outside of the polygon, turning at each corner to follow the next side.
Add up all the turns you make to get back to your starting direction.
Repeat for convex polygons with different numbers of sides and confirm the turns always total exactly 360°, however many sides there are.
At a single chosen corner, mark the interior angle and the exterior angle sitting together on a straight line, and check they sum to 180°.
Say aloud the difference between the two totals: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex; ALL exterior angles together = 360° for the whole polygon.
activities.intendedInsight: Walking the perimeter of a convex polygon means turning through one full 360° in total, so the exterior angles sum to 360°, regardless of the number of sides — a separate fact from the 180° interior/exterior pair at a single vertex.

activities.title: Regular or irregular: when may you divide by n?
feedback: If a learner divides an irregular polygon's sum by n, point to two visibly different angles in the figure and ask whether they could both equal the quotient; contrast directly with the regular hexagon of the same 720° sum where every angle really is 120°.

If a learner reports 540° as a single interior angle of the pentagon, ask 'is 540° a sensible size for ONE angle in a pentagon?' and prompt the final ÷5 — the method is sound, only the last step was dropped.
An optional regular/irregular toggle where the '÷n' button is available only in regular mode makes the boundary visible; the greying-out illustrates the condition, it does not prove it.
activities.rationale: The equal-angles condition, which every regular polygon meets, is the distinction the topic hinges on. Holding the sum fixed (same-sided regular vs irregular hexagon) and keeping the subtract-from-sum method alongside the ÷n method prevents over-generalising ÷n and separately addresses the forget-to-divide lapse.
sourceClaims: Students commonly confuse interior and exterior angles; they wrongly assume all exterior angles are equal or that more sides means a bigger exterior sum (it is always 360° regardless of the number of sides); the formula 360÷n gives each exterior angle ONLY for a regular polygon — irregular polygons still total 360° but each angle must be found individually
learnerActions: Take a regular pentagon: find the interior sum by triangulation (3×180 = 540°), then find EACH interior angle by dividing by n (540÷5 = 108°).
Find each exterior angle two ways and check they agree: 180 − 108 = 72° and 360÷5 = 72°.

Compare two hexagons that have the SAME interior sum of 720°: a regular hexagon, where ÷6 gives each angle = 720÷6 = 120°, and an irregular hexagon, where the angles are visibly unequal so no single quotient describes them all.

For the irregular hexagon, divide 720 by 6 to get 120°, then compare with the figure: its angles are not all equal, so 120° cannot be each angle — ÷n does not give each angle of a polygon whose angles are unequal (even if one angle happened to equal the quotient).
Instead, find ONE missing angle of the irregular hexagon by subtracting the five known angles from 720°.

Write the rule: you may divide the sum by n to get each angle ONLY when every angle is equal, as in every regular polygon (a rectangle shows that equal angles are enough, even if the sides differ); the sum itself is the same for any hexagon.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing the interior sum by n (or using 360÷n for exterior) gives each angle ONLY when all the angles are equal, as in a regular polygon. Two polygons with the same number of sides share the same interior sum, but for one with unequal angles a missing angle is found by subtracting the known angles rather than by dividing.

activities.title: Triangle angle sum: 180°, not 360°
feedback: If a learner gives 360 − 70 − 60 = 230°, they are treating the triangle's angles as going 'all the way round' to 360° — re-derive 180° from the torn corners on a straight edge and contrast with a full turn.

Note for the teacher: tearing corners DEMONSTRATES the 180° sum but is not a proof; pupils should also meet the deductive argument (e.g. draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and use alternate angles).
activities.rationale: The 'triangle sums to 360°' error is documented, and this activity both corrects it and distinguishes demonstration from proof as the pedagogy requires. The torn-corner task is concrete physical evidence; its status as demonstration (not proof) is stated.
sourceClaims: A common documented misconception on a triangle missing-angle item is that the angles sum to 360° (subtracting the known angles from 360)

The interior angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n−2)×180°, derived by splitting the polygon into n−2 triangles each summing to 180° (quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°); an exterior angle is on a straight line with its interior angle so they sum to 180°; the sum of all exterior angles is 360° (from 180n − (n−2)×180 = 360); students often confuse a demonstration for a proof
learnerActions: Find the third angle of a triangle whose other two angles are 70° and 60° by subtracting from 180°: 180 − 70 − 60 = 50°.
Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and arrange them against a straight edge; observe they fit along a straight line (180°).
Contrast this straight-line 180° with a full turn of 360° so the two 'wholes' are kept apart.
Explain why you subtracted from 180° and not 360°.
activities.intendedInsight: A triangle's interior angles sum to 180° (a straight line), which is a different whole from the 360° of a full turn; a missing angle is found by subtracting the known angles from 180°.

activities.title: Check and consolidate with mixed questions
feedback: If a learner picks the option that divides an irregular polygon's sum by n, revisit the regular/irregular distinction: ÷n needs equal angles.
If a learner selects an exterior angle when asked for an interior one, return to the straight-line pair at a vertex (they sum to 180°).

Scored questions confirm whether the facts and distinctions are secure, but on their own they do not show the learner deriving the sum by triangulation or reasoning openly about interior/exterior — pair them with the construction activities.
activities.rationale: Structured questions check fluency and surface the exact distractors (irregular ÷n, interior/exterior swap) the topic targets. They are proposed as a complement to, not a replacement for, the derivation work.
sourceClaims: Students commonly confuse interior and exterior angles; they wrongly assume all exterior angles are equal or that more sides means a bigger exterior sum (it is always 360° regardless of the number of sides); the formula 360÷n gives each exterior angle ONLY for a regular polygon — irregular polygons still total 360° but each angle must be found individually
learnerActions: Give the interior-angle sum of a named polygon (e.g. octagon → (8−2)×180 = 1080°).
For a regular polygon, give BOTH an interior angle and its matching exterior angle, and state how they relate (sum to 180° at a vertex).
Answer a question that contrasts interior versus exterior angles, and identify why a tempting wrong option (dividing the sum by n for an irregular polygon whose angles are unequal) is invalid.
Order several polygons by their interior-angle sum and explain what the ordering depends on (number of sides).
activities.intendedInsight: Named-polygon sums, interior/exterior relationships and the regular-only condition can be recalled and applied fluently and distinguished from common distractors.

constraints: Division by n (sum÷n for each interior, 360÷n for each exterior) gives each angle ONLY when all the angles are equal. Every regular polygon has equal angles, and regular polygons are the KS3 focus, but some irregular shapes do too: a non-square rectangle has four 90° angles (360÷4). For polygons with unequal angles, find a missing angle by subtracting the known angles from the sum. Never present ÷n as giving each angle of a polygon whose angles are unequal.

Two polygons with the same number of sides have the same interior-angle sum. Whether all the angles are equal (as in any regular polygon) affects only whether each angle equals sum÷n, not the sum itself.
Keep the two totals distinct: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex; ALL exterior angles together = 360° for the whole polygon.
Tearing off triangle corners onto a straight line DEMONSTRATES the 180° sum; it is not a proof. Pupils should also meet the deductive argument.
The angle sum depends on the number of sides, not on the polygon's size; an enlarged copy of the same shape has the same angles.

When a convex polygon is split from one vertex, an n-sided polygon yields n−2 triangles (not n); diagonals are drawn only from the single chosen vertex, and the two sides meeting at that vertex do not each form a separate triangle base.
The perimeter-walk 'one full turn = 360°' model applies to convex (non-reflex) polygons, the intended KS3 case; the interior-sum (n−2)×180° and subtract-from-sum methods hold for any simple polygon.

Fixed diagrams (tap-to-reveal) can show one triangle split and label interior/exterior at a vertex but cannot let the child vary n or test the regular/irregular boundary; treat them as support, not as inferior in every respect.
Scored/recognition questions assess facts and distinctions but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own triangulation or open interior/exterior reasoning; pair them with construction work.
Polygon angle sums are planar; polyhedron angle defect is a different, later topic and is not needed here.

Optional interactive features (running sum as diagonals are drawn, perimeter-walk accumulator, regular/irregular toggle with ÷n button enabled only in regular mode) are illustrations of the mechanism, not mandatory tools and not evidence that the rules hold.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists the KS3 national curriculum citation as verified:false; its claim is used only to describe curriculum expectations, not to assert efficacy.

Self-audit (arithmetic/geometry) checks passed and were retained: triangle 180−70−60=50°; pentagon 3×180=540°, 540÷5=108°, exterior 180−108=72°=360÷5; hexagon 4×180=720°, regular hexagon 720÷6=120°; octagon (8−2)×180=1080°; exterior-sum identity 180n−(n−2)×180=360.

Corrected an overstated claim in the regular/irregular activity: dividing an irregular hexagon's 720° by 6 need not differ from EVERY angle (one angle could coincidentally be 120°); the valid point is that a single quotient cannot describe unequal angles, so ÷n does not apply.

The perimeter-walk one-full-turn model assumes convex polygons; learner examples here are convex, which is the standard KS3 case. The (n−2)×180° interior-sum derivation and the subtract-from-sum method remain valid for any simple polygon.

Original row asserts '3D adds nothing' and that unscripted dialogue 'neither performs the triangulation nor checks the arithmetic' as fit rationales; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established comparative claims, and have been softened to narrowly scoped limits in constraints rather than propagated as universal laws.
The Hart et al. (2018) source concerns triangle size-independence specifically; it is extended here to polygon size-independence, which the source does not directly establish for all polygons.

Retained the original key representation of a regular polygon beside an irregular one with the SAME sum but unequal angles (regular vs irregular hexagon at 720°); no mathematical error was found in that content.

probeDeeper: 'If I made this pentagon twice as big, would each angle change? Why or why not?' — a counterexample targeting size-dependence
'You split the hexagon into 4 triangles — why 4 and not 6?' — pushing the (n−2) structure into a reason
'This hexagon is irregular — can you still divide 720 by 6 to get each angle? Why not?' — a counterexample on the regular-only division
'At this corner, how are the interior and exterior angles related, and how do you know?' — pressing the 180°-at-a-vertex link
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 180 − 70 − 60 = 50°. (b) The hexagon splits into 4 triangles from one vertex, so the interior sum is 4×180 = 720°; a missing angle is 720 minus the other five. (c) Regular pentagon interior sum = 3×180 = 540°, so each interior angle = 540÷5 = 108°; each exterior angle = 180 − 108 = 72° (equivalently 360÷5 = 72°). The child derives the sum by triangulation and divides by n only because the pentagon is stated to be regular.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a triangle's angles sum to 360° — subtracts the known angles from 360 ('shapes go all the way round to 360')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-derive triangle = 180° from the straight line (tear the three corners onto a straight edge); contrast with the 360° of a full turn so the two wholes are kept apart
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (a) gives 360−70−60 = 230°, or any answer built on a 360° whole for the triangle

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses interior and exterior angles — gives the exterior when asked for the interior (or vice versa), or treats them as unrelated rather than summing to 180° at the vertex
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the interior and exterior angle at one vertex sitting on a straight line so they must sum to 180°; label both on the same diagram before calculating
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (c) reports 72° as 'the interior angle' or 108° as 'the exterior', or cannot connect the two at a vertex

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides by n for an IRREGULAR polygon, or assumes all its angles are equal — applies 360÷n or sum÷n without checking regularity
errorPatterns.nextMove: Stress that ÷n gives each angle ONLY when the polygon is regular; for an irregular one, find a missing angle by subtracting the known angles from the sum
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (b) divides 720 by 6 to 'find each angle' of the irregular hexagon, though its angles differ

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes the angle sum depends on the polygon's SIZE — a bigger triangle/polygon has bigger angles ('the longer side makes a wider angle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the same-shape polygon enlarged with its angles unchanged; make explicit that the sum depends only on the number of sides, not the size
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Judges or adjusts an angle according to side length or overall size rather than using the fixed sum

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the interior-angle SUM as if it were a single interior angle — forgets to divide by n for the regular polygon
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'is 540° a sensible size for ONE angle in a pentagon?'; prompt the final ÷5 — the method is right, only the last step was dropped, so scaffold rather than reteach
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (c) gives 540° as 'each interior angle' of the pentagon instead of 540÷5 = 108°

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find the angles reliably — sums a triangle to 360°, cannot derive a polygon's angle sum, or divides an irregular polygon's sum by n; interior and exterior are confused
responseLevels.full: Derives the interior-angle sum by splitting into n−2 triangles, calculates interior and exterior angles keeping the two distinct, divides by n only for regular polygons, and explains that the sum depends on the number of sides not the size — transferring the method to a polygon with a new number of sides
responseLevels.partial: Uses 180° for the triangle and can recall or apply (n−2)×180° for the sum, but cannot derive it by triangulation, forgets to divide by n (or divides when the polygon is irregular), or confuses interior with exterior — has the formulas as isolated rules, not a connected structure, and cannot transfer to a new polygon or justify why

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three figures and a pencil: (a) a triangle with two angles marked 70° and 60°; (b) an IRREGULAR hexagon; (c) a regular pentagon. Set them to: (a) find the third angle; (b) find the sum of the interior angles of the hexagon, showing how — invite them to split it up — then find one missing angle given the other five; (c) find EACH interior angle and EACH exterior angle of the regular pentagon. Watch whether they subtract from 180 (not 360) for the triangle, whether they split the hexagon into triangles to get (n−2)×180, whether they divide by n only because the pentagon is regular, and whether they keep interior and exterior angles distinct.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands subtracts the triangle's angles from 180 and derives the hexagon sum by triangulating; a child with the classic error subtracts from 360 (a visibly different answer) or divides the irregular hexagon's sum by 6. Asking for EACH angle of the regular pentagon and its exterior angle exposes interior/exterior confusion and the forget-to-÷n lapse; the irregular hexagon exposes those who apply ÷n indiscriminately.
